summary: Describes five types of SNMP applications that make use of an SNMP engine, and defines MIB modules for specifying targets of management operations, notification filtering and proxy forwarding. It obsoletes RFC 2273 and was replaced by RFC 3413.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes the different jobs a network-monitoring tool can do, like asking questions and sending alerts, and how to say who gets which alert.

questions: what is the difference between snmp trap and inform
what is an snmp proxy forwarder
subtitle: The five kinds of SNMP application, and the MIB modules that say where notifications go and how proxies forward.

tldr.problem: SNMP engines handle messages, but something has to sit on top to send requests, answer them, send and receive notifications, and forward messages, and notification senders and proxies need a way to know where and how to send.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five application types (command generator, command responder, notification originator, notification receiver, proxy forwarder) with their procedures, and three MIB modules for management targets, notification filtering and proxy forwarding.
tldr.outcome: It was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 2273 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3413.

today: RFC 2573 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 2273, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3413, which is the current text to read.

sections.title: Five Kinds of SNMP Application
sections.content:
An SNMP engine moves and secures messages; applications sit on top of it. This RFC describes five types. A command generator initiates Read-Class and/or Write-Class requests and processes the responses. A command responder receives such requests and answers them under access control. A notification originator watches for events and sends Notification-Class messages. A notification receiver listens for them and replies when a message carries a Confirmed-Class PDU. A proxy forwarder forwards SNMP messages.

There are no restrictions on combining types: one engine can host both a command generator and a command responder. Proxy forwarding is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a school office: some people ask questions, some answer, some ring alarms, some listen for alarms, and some pass notes along.

sections.title: Command Generators and Responders
sections.content:
Applications talk to the engine's Dispatcher through abstract service interfaces. A command generator calls sendPdu, naming the transport domain and address, message processing model, security model, security name and level, context and the PDU. It keeps the returned sendPduHandle to match the reply. A response is discarded if its security and context values or its request-id differ from the original request.

A command responder first registers a contextEngineID and PDU types with the engine. When a request arrives, it performs the operation against the MIB view allowed by the security level, model, context and name, checking each object with isAccessAllowed. Access failures become an authorization error in the response. An unknown context increments the snmpUnknownContexts counter, and an unavailable one increments snmpUnavailableContexts. In both cases no result PDU is generated. It should always call returnResponsePdu to answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The asker writes a numbered question and remembers the number. The answerer checks the asker is allowed to know, then replies with the same number.

sections.title: Notifications: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
A notification originator picks the targets for each notification, applies filters, retrieves the variable-bindings allowed by the target's MIB view, checks the notification's snmpTrapOID.0 against access control, and builds a PDU. Unconfirmed-Class notifications are sent once. For Confirmed-Class ones the originator caches the target, waits for a response, and retries up to the retry count before giving up.

A notification receiver registers with a wildcard context engine ID and the notification PDU types it wants. For an Unconfirmed-Class PDU, what happens next depends on the implementation. For a Confirmed-Class PDU it builds a Response with the same request-id and variable-bindings and with error-status and error-index both 0, and returns it.
sections.plainLanguage: An alarm either gets shouted once, or shouted until someone says "I heard you", up to a set number of tries.

sections.title: Proxy Forwarders
sections.content:
This RFC uses "proxy" in a tight sense: forwarding SNMP messages to other engines based on the context, regardless of which managed objects they touch. A traditional agent's command responder, which works object by object, is not a proxy in this sense.

To forward a request, the proxy registers the context engine IDs it handles, translates the incoming management target into one outgoing target, builds a new PDU with a fresh request-id and caches what it needs to match the reply. If no outgoing target exists, it increments snmpProxyDrops and returns an error indication. When the response comes back, the proxy finds the cache entry, restores the original request-id and returns the response to the original sender. Internal-class PDUs such as Report are forwarded back the same way, unless the original SNMP version does not support Report PDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy is a mail forwarder: it puts your letter in a new envelope, remembers who sent it, and hands the reply back to you.

sections.title: The Three MIB Modules
sections.content:
A management target is destination information (a transport domain and address) plus SNMP parameters (message processing model, security model, level and name). The SNMP-TARGET-MIB holds these in snmpTargetAddrTable and snmpTargetParamsTable, in a many-to-many relationship. Address entries are grouped by tags in snmpTargetAddrTagList.

The notification MIB uses snmpNotifyTable to select targets by tag. Its snmpNotifyType chooses trap(1) (Unconfirmed-Class) or inform(2) (Confirmed-Class). Filtering uses snmpNotifyFilterTable to include or exclude subtrees. The proxy MIB holds the translation table a proxy uses. An implementation that makes this configuration SNMP-manageable MUST use the matching module.
sections.plainLanguage: These are address books: one says where messages go and how to send them, one says who gets which alert, and one says where a proxy passes things on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: These applications have direct access to MIB instrumentation, so they must apply access control strictly. Notification generators that get MIB data by other means, for example from a command line, must not reveal information that access control would normally hide. The MIBs themselves hold potentially sensitive information, and an administrator may want to limit access to them.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can see the network's secrets must follow the rules about who is allowed to know what.

items.title: Proxy forwarder
items.text: Forwards messages by context, not by object.
